title: Campaign: migrations and rollout across the estate
_note: rv2 S2 (PLAN §2.2 campaign-<tag> row, tag migrations-rollout). Sources are 3 live campaign study quests from different repos per idea; recapAfter = any 3 sources passed. Server-local side file, never stamped.

ideas.idea: Ship a schema change as a series of deploys: widen the schema, write both shapes, copy old rows in batches, move reads, stop old writes, then narrow it.
ideas.why: Doing a rename or a required column in one deploy breaks whichever app version is still running during the rollout.
ideas.prompt: A team wants to add a required column and rename another in one migration that runs at deploy. The app runs on several instances with rolling restarts. Lay out a safer sequence.
ideas.answer: Add the new column as nullable or with a default and keep the old one. Write both from the new code, backfill old rows in batches from a job, switch reads (behind a flag if possible), stop writing the old column, and drop it in a later deploy. Each step works with the previous app version still serving.

ideas.idea: A migration is code that runs against production data: generate it, read the SQL it produces, and never edit one that has already been applied.
ideas.why: Generated migrations can drop and recreate tables, and changing an applied file makes environments disagree about the schema.
ideas.prompt: Someone adds a comment line to a migration file that was applied yesterday, and another developer's generated migration for a renamed property drops a column. What should the team's rules be?
ideas.answer: Applied migrations are immutable: changes go into a new migration, and the runner should refuse a changed checksum. Every generated migration is read before merge, because a rename can come out as drop plus add, which loses data; rewrite it as a rename or an expand-contract sequence.

ideas.idea: Roll a change out with a flag that buckets users by a stable hash, and define the edges exactly: 0% means nobody, 100% means everyone.
ideas.why: Unstable or off-by-one bucketing flips users between old and new behaviour, or lets a 0% flag reach some users.
ideas.prompt: A percentage rollout set to 0% still enables the feature for a few customers. The bucket comes from a hash modulo 100 compared with the percentage. What do you check?
ideas.answer: The comparison at the edges: buckets run 0 to 99, so 'bucket <= percentage' admits bucket 0 at 0%; use 'bucket < percentage'. Check the hash is stable across processes and deploys, and that the evaluation reports why a user is in or out, so support can explain it.

ideas.idea: When moving data to a new store, write to both and read from the old one until the new one is verified, then switch reads behind a flag.
ideas.why: Switching in one step leaves no way back, and a crash between the two writes of a dual write leaves the stores disagreeing silently.
ideas.prompt: Analytics events move from Postgres to a column store. A consumer inserts a batch into the new store and then acknowledges it. Where is the batch if the process dies between those two steps, and how do you plan the move?
ideas.answer: Inserted but not acknowledged, so it will be redelivered and inserted twice unless inserts are idempotent by event id. Plan the move as dual writes with idempotent inserts, read from the old store while you compare counts, flip reads with a flag, and keep the old path until the new one is proven.

ideas.idea: When a release changes the shape of data stored on clients, migrate on first load, keep a backup of the old payload, and stay able to read both versions.
ideas.why: A migration that overwrites local data in place cannot be undone when it has a bug, and users lose progress that exists nowhere else.
ideas.prompt: Version 2 of an app changes the shape of progress data kept in localStorage. What should the first load after the release do, and what could go wrong otherwise?
ideas.answer: Read the stored payload, detect its version, save the raw v1 data under a backup key, then write the migrated v2 data under the main key. If the migration code is wrong, the backup lets a fix restore it. Without that, a buggy migration overwrites the only copy of the user's progress.
